parts.markdown:
Use our free **Kansas paycheck calculator** to estimate your take-home pay after federal income tax, Kansas income tax, Social Security, Medicare and other payroll deductions.

Enter your annual salary or hourly wage, select your payment frequency and customize your withholding information to see how much money you could receive on payday.

Kansas uses a progressive state income tax structure with withholding allowances that can significantly affect your paycheck. Understanding these rules can help you compare employment opportunities, assess salary increases and establish a realistic household budget.

Whether you work in Wichita, Topeka, Overland Park, Lawrence or another Kansas community, this calculator provides a practical starting point for understanding your earnings.

## How to Use the Kansas Paycheck Calculator

Select annual salary if you receive fixed compensation or hourly wages if your earnings depend on working hours.

Enter your gross compensation before taxes and choose your payment frequency.

Enter federal and Kansas income tax withheld for the pay period from your pay stub.

Include retirement contributions and healthcare premiums. Enter the full withholding amounts, including any additional withholding.

If your earnings are approaching an annual federal payroll contribution limit, enter your year-to-date taxable wages.

Review your estimated paycheck breakdown to understand how each deduction affects your net earnings.

For greater accuracy, use the information shown on your latest pay stub and withholding certificates.

## Kansas Payroll Taxes in 2026

Kansas employees generally face federal and state income taxes alongside ordinary federal payroll contributions.

Kansas municipalities generally do not impose separate personal wage income taxes. However, employees working across state borders may encounter different local tax requirements.

Your actual paycheck depends on taxable earnings, withholding allowances, payment frequency and employee benefit deductions.

## How Kansas State Income Tax Works

Kansas applies progressive income tax rates, meaning higher portions of taxable income may be subject to higher rates.

The state's current employer withholding framework uses rates of 5.2% and 5.58%, with a zero-withholding range below applicable thresholds.

Employees should not multiply their entire annual salary by 5.58% when estimating state withholding.

Kansas employers must first account for qualifying withholding allowances and then apply the appropriate payroll-period calculation.

The [Kansas Department of Revenue withholding guide](https://www.ksrevenue.gov/kw100.html) provides the official methodology and withholding tables.

## Kansas Withholding Allowances

Kansas recognizes different annual withholding allowances based on the employee's applicable withholding classification.

The allowance amount is divided by the number of annual pay periods before being applied to the current paycheck.

For example, an employee entitled to a $9,160 annual allowance and paid biweekly receives an allowance adjustment of approximately $352.31 per paycheck.

These allowances help determine payroll withholding rather than necessarily representing every deduction or exemption available on an annual income tax return.

Employees should confirm their applicable allowances when completing Kansas Form K-4.

## Understanding Kansas Form K-4

Kansas employees generally use Form K-4 to provide state withholding information to their employers.

Your selections help determine the applicable withholding classification, allowances and additional withholding amounts.

Federal Form W-4 and Kansas Form K-4 are separate documents. Updating your federal withholding elections does not automatically update your Kansas withholding information.

Married employees with working spouses should review the form's instructions rather than assuming both employers can apply the full joint allowance.

Employees who qualify for exemption from withholding must satisfy the applicable requirements.

Visit the [Kansas Department of Revenue](https://www.ksrevenue.gov/) for current withholding forms and instructions.

## Kansas Income Tax Withholding Example

Consider an employee receiving $2,500 in biweekly Kansas taxable wages.

Assume the employee uses the single withholding classification, qualifies for a $9,160 annual allowance and has no additional dependent allowances or withholding.

First, calculate the biweekly allowance:

$9,160 ÷ 26 = approximately $352.31

Next, subtract this allowance from taxable wages:

$2,500 − $352.31 = $2,147.69

Under the Kansas biweekly single withholding percentage table, adjusted earnings exceeding $1,023 are calculated using a base amount of $46 plus 5.58% of the excess.

Estimated withholding:

$46 + (($2,147.69 − $1,023) × 0.0558)

Kansas withholding is approximately $108.76.

Your employer may use an authorized rounding method or wage bracket table that produces a slightly different result.

## Federal Taxes Deducted From Kansas Paychecks

### Federal income tax

Federal income tax withholding depends on taxable wages, filing status, payroll frequency and information supplied on Form W-4.

Employees with multiple jobs, eligible tax credits or other sources of income may need additional withholding adjustments.

The official calculation procedures are available in [IRS Publication 15-T](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15t).

### Social Security

Employees generally contribute 6.2% of covered earnings toward Social Security.

For 2026, the annual taxable wage ceiling is $184,500.

An employee receiving $2,500 in covered wages who has not reached the annual limit would contribute $155.

### Medicare

Ordinary Medicare withholding applies at 1.45% of covered wages.

Unlike Social Security, Medicare does not have a standard annual wage ceiling.

Employers generally withhold an additional 0.9% when Medicare-covered wages paid by that employer exceed $200,000 during the calendar year.

The [IRS Employer's Tax Guide](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15) explains these payroll contribution requirements.

## Kansas Hourly Paycheck Calculator

Hourly employees can estimate gross earnings by multiplying their hourly wage by regular hours and adding qualifying overtime compensation.

Suppose an employee earns $26 per hour and works 40 regular hours plus five qualifying overtime hours at time-and-a-half.

Regular earnings:

$26 × 40 = $1,040

Overtime earnings:

$26 × 1.5 × 5 = $195

Total gross earnings:

$1,235

Federal taxes, Kansas withholding and payroll deductions are then calculated using the relevant taxable wage amounts.

Overtime eligibility depends on employment classification and applicable federal and state labor laws.

Consult the [Kansas Department of Labor](https://www.dol.ks.gov/) and [US Department of Labor overtime guidance](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime) for additional information.

## Working in Kansas and Missouri

The Kansas City metropolitan area extends across Kansas and Missouri, making interstate employment relatively common.

An employee may live in Kansas while working for a Missouri employer or perform employment duties in both states.

Kansas and Missouri do not have a general reciprocal wage income tax agreement.

Employees may therefore have withholding or filing responsibilities in both states, with applicable resident tax credits potentially reducing double taxation.

Kansas City, Missouri, also has an earnings tax that may affect qualifying employees working there. Do not confuse Kansas City, Kansas, with Kansas City, Missouri, when entering employment information.

Consult the relevant state tax agencies and the [Kansas City, Missouri, government](https://www.kcmo.gov/) for applicable local tax requirements.

## How Employee Benefits Affect Kansas Take-Home Pay

Retirement contributions, healthcare premiums and other employee benefits can influence your net paycheck.

Traditional retirement contributions generally reduce current federal income-taxable wages. Roth contributions generally do not provide the same immediate income tax reduction.

Qualifying health benefits may reduce certain taxable wage amounts.

However, these deductions may affect income tax and federal payroll contribution bases differently.

Review your pay stub to confirm how each benefit is classified.

When comparing job offers, consider the employer's retirement match, healthcare coverage, paid leave and insurance costs alongside your estimated take-home salary.

## Planning Your Kansas Monthly Budget

Use your estimated net income to establish spending limits for housing, transportation, groceries, utilities, insurance and required debt payments.

If you receive biweekly paychecks, remember that the standard 26 annual payments do not translate into exactly two paychecks every month.

Use our [emergency fund calculator](/savings/emergency-fund-calculator/) to evaluate your savings target and our [salary-to-hourly calculator](/calculators/salary-to-hourly-calculator/) to compare different compensation arrangements.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the Kansas income tax rate in 2026?

The applicable Kansas employer withholding framework uses rates of 5.2% and 5.58%, with thresholds and allowances that determine the actual amount deducted.

### Does Kansas have local employee income taxes?

Kansas municipalities generally do not impose ordinary personal wage income taxes. However, Kansas residents working in another state may encounter local taxes in their employment jurisdiction.

### Why do married employees sometimes have different Kansas withholding amounts?

Different withholding classifications and allowances can affect the taxable amount used in the payroll calculation. Working spouses may also need to adjust withholding to account for combined household income.
